headlines.full_text: Yemen targets Saudi Arabia’s financial hub The Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF) targeted the financial district in the Saudi capital on Thursday. The attack on the Saudi hallmark came as YAF makes battlefield advances against the Saudi-backed forces inside Yemen. The Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF) targeted the financial district in the Saudi capital on Thursday. The attack on the Saudi hallmark came as YAF makes battlefield advances against the Saudi-backed forces inside Yemen. The YAF struck Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, which houses the headquarters of the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF), the sovereign wealth fund that finances the kingdom’s mega-projects in line with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 initiative. The attack shattered windows across seven to eight floors of the Public Investment Fund tower and bent sections of its metal façade, Alhurra reported. It was the second time in less than two weeks that a YAF attack had damaged a prominent building in Riyadh’s financial district. The earlier strike on Nov. 8 targeted an administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco, the kingdom’s state-owned oil giant. Saudi Civil Defense said in a statement that the tower was partly damaged but that there had been no injuries. Entrances to the King Abdullah Financial District were closed on Thursday, and people were evacuated as ambulances and fire engines gathered at the scene. The Saudi-led forces said in a statement that they had dealt with a “missile threat” launched by YAF toward Riyadh. YAF has been firing missiles at Saudi airports and oil infrastructure since the war in Yemen resumed in July. Held under the slogan “Progressive Iran,” the CITEX exhibition took place at Milad Tower in Tehran from November 17 to 20. More than 100 knowledge-based companies gathered at the event, hosted by Tehran Municipality, to help establish an integrated ecosystem for urban technology and innovation. Transportation, municipal services, energy, water and the environment, and information technology were among the event’s main themes. Energy management, waste management, the digital economy, and sustainable financing for urban projects were also addressed. Companies and industry professionals active in fintech, municipal services and citizen welfare, smart transportation and traffic management, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, ICT infrastructure, water management, agriculture, and the urban environment showcased their latest achievements and ideas. Mohebbi recalled that the late Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, had previously set a 2,000-kilometer limit on the range of Iranian missiles. However, he stressed that Iran is capable of striking US military installations in Europe if a new order is issued. He also referred to Iran's previously demonstrated missile capabilities, citing a reported range of 4,500 kilometers, which he said places the US-British military base on Diego Garcia within reach. In a post on his X account, Baqaei said the allegations reflect a familiar US narrative that has shifted from claims of an Iranian nuclear threat to accusations of chemical and biological weapons development. He questioned whether US officials expected the international community to forget the 2003 appearance of then-Secretary of State Colin Powell before the UN Security Council, when he displayed a small vial as purported evidence of Iraq's weapons of mass destruction program. Baqaei described the episode as one of the most consequential intelligence failures and political deceptions in modern history, noting that unsubstantiated claims about Iraq's possession of weapons of mass destruction were deliberately used to generate public support for a military invasion. He stressed that the consequences of the invasion were catastrophic, affecting not only the Iraqi people but also the wider region and American society. headlines.full_text: The limits of military power and the fiction of ‘finishing the job’ MADRID - In recent weeks, the narrative calling for “finishing the job” in Iran has resurfaced, more a propaganda slogan than a concrete strategy. MADRID - In recent weeks, the narrative calling for “finishing the job” in Iran has resurfaced, more a propaganda slogan than a concrete strategy. First, there is no consensus on what the objective actually is. Some talk of regime change. For others, it means destroying the ballistic missiles Iran still holds, ending its nuclear program and its support for the Axis of Resistance, seizing its enriched uranium or ending its exclusive control of the Strait of Hormuz. And for a third group, it means achieving all of these goals at once. This narrative claims, without explaining how, that a new military operation can achieve what was not achieved in 40 days of war. If anything has become clear since that war, it is that Iran is not going to collapse, despite the many attempts to bring it about. It has also shown that it has no intention of surrendering. And there is little reason to believe that air power alone can topple the Islamic Republic, even if the United States and Israel strike Iran’s energy infrastructure. Such attacks would almost certainly provoke a harsh Iranian retaliation against energy facilities across the region, with potentially devastating consequences for global energy markets. Moreover, both Israel and the United States have reached the limits of their military power. headlines.full_text: War on Iran leaves Arab monarchies facing $1 trillion in losses TEHRAN — The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran will cost the six Arab monarchies in the Persian Gulf nearly $1 trillion in destroyed infrastructure and lost economic output through 2030, Allianz Research estimates, leaving governments to borrow heavily and redirect wealth once invested abroad toward repairs and protection at home. TEHRAN — The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran will cost the six Arab monarchies in the Persian Gulf nearly $1 trillion in destroyed infrastructure and lost economic output through 2030, Allianz Research estimates, leaving governments to borrow heavily and redirect wealth once invested abroad toward repairs and protection at home. Its November report projects $790 billion in output losses over 2026–30, alongside just over $200 billion in physical damage. The output figure measures the gap against the prewar growth trajectory. More than 80 energy facilities have been hit, about one-third severely, although most production infrastructure escaped major damage. Geography determines who suffers most. Allianz forecasts a 4% contraction across the Persian Gulf Cooperation Council this year, with Hormuz-dependent Qatar shrinking 14%, Kuwait 11% and Bahrain 8%. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, which have tried to bypass the strait for some exports, contract 2.8% and 0.9%. Oman grows 3.3%, benefiting from its alternative ports. Recovery will take longer than reopening shipping lanes. Damage affecting roughly 18% of Qatar’s gas output will take years to repair. Tourist arrivals fell 22% in the first half, while Dubai home prices dropped 10.2% from January’s peak by September. Allianz expects tourism to approach prewar levels only in 2029. The consequences reach government balance sheets. Cumulative budget deficits are forecast at $475 billion; maturing debt raises financing requirement
headlines.llm_reasoning: It reports economic estimates from Allianz Research, presenting data neutrally.
